title: SQL Interview & OA Questions
relevance: Classic SQL problems and theory that appear repeatedly in SDE interviews and OAs at companies like Amazon, Google, Meta, and top startups.
company_notes: Asked at Amazon, Google, Meta, and top startups.

phases.goal: Establish core SELECT/WHERE/aggregate patterns and basic SQL theory distinctions.

must_hit.point: A self join aliases the same employees table as e and m, joining e.manager_id to m.emp_id to compare salaries.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes employees aliased twice and the join linking each employee to their manager for salary comparison.

must_hit.point: HAVING filters after aggregation; WHERE filters individual rows before grouping.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts WHERE (pre-GROUP BY) with HAVING (post-aggregation), e.g. departments with headcount above a threshold.

must_hit.point: Customers with no orders can be found via LEFT JOIN plus IS NULL, or via NOT EXISTS.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names either LEFT JOIN/IS NULL or NOT EXISTS and explains filtering for absence of matching orders.

must_hit.point: Duplicate emails are found by GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1, then optionally pulling full rows via those emails.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate aggregates on the suspected duplicate column and filters groups with count greater than one.

probes: How would you find employees who earn more than their manager?
What's the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
How do you find customers who never placed an order?

hints.1: Think about joining a table to itself, or filtering after you group.
hints.2: Self join on manager_id; HAVING after COUNT; LEFT JOIN/IS NULL or NOT EXISTS for missing orders.
hints.3: Alias employees as e and m on e.manager_id = m.emp_id WHERE e.salary > m.salary; HAVING filters post-aggregation; NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe vs NOT IN.

phases.goal: Show how joins, window functions, CASE pivots, and ranking framing actually work.

must_hit.point: DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) then filter rnk = 2 finds the second-highest salary and handles ties; MAX subquery with salary < max only works for second highest.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate prefers DENSE_RANK for ties and Nth-highest extensibility, and may mention the MAX-of-less-than-max pattern for second only.

must_hit.point: PARTITION BY dept_id with DENSE_RANK finds the Nth highest per department; DENSE_RANK gives no gap after ties unlike RANK.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains independent ranking windows per department and why DENSE_RANK avoids skipping ranks after ties.

must_hit.point: ROW_NUMBER() with PARTITION BY customer_id and rn <= 3 returns exactly top N rows per group even when totals tie.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate chooses ROW_NUMBER over RANK/DENSE_RANK when they need a fixed row count despite identical values.

must_hit.point: SUM(CASE WHEN quarter = 'Q1' THEN revenue ELSE 0 END) pivots quarterly rows into columns without vendor-specific PIVOT.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes the SUM(CASE ...) pattern grouping by product for Q1–Q4 columns.

must_hit.point: LAG looks back within a window; NULLIF on prior amount avoids division by zero in year-over-year growth.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate mentions LAG partitioned by month ordered by year and NULLIF guarding the growth percentage.

probes: How do you find the second-highest salary? What if there are ties?
How would you get the top 3 orders per customer?
How do you pivot quarters from rows into columns in plain SQL?

hints.1: Window ranking and framing matter more than LIMIT/OFFSET here.
hints.2: DENSE_RANK for Nth salary; ROW_NUMBER for exact top-N rows; SUM(CASE) for pivot; LAG plus NULLIF for YoY.
hints.3: DENSE_RANK OVER ORDER BY salary DESC WHERE rnk = 2; ROW_NUMBER PARTITION BY customer_id WHERE rn <= 3; SUM(CASE WHEN quarter = 'Q1' ...); LAG with NULLIF(..., 0).

phases.goal: Compare alternate SQL approaches and ranking/index/set-operator tradeoffs from the bank.

must_hit.point: LEFT JOIN + IS NULL is often the fastest plan for missing matches; NOT EXISTS has cleaner semantics and is strictly NULL-safe versus NOT IN.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts execution-plan speed of LEFT JOIN/IS NULL with readability and NULL-safety of NOT EXISTS.

must_hit.point: Avoid LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 for second-highest salary because ties for the highest can skip the wrong row.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate rejects OFFSET-based second-highest and prefers DENSE_RANK or the MAX-subquery approach.

must_hit.point: On ties, ROW_NUMBER assigns 1, 2, 3; RANK assigns 1, 1, 3 leaving a gap; DENSE_RANK assigns 1, 1, 2 with no gap.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate correctly states the three tie behaviors with those rank sequences.

must_hit.point: UNION deduplicates (slower); UNION ALL keeps duplicates (faster).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names dedup cost of UNION versus speed of UNION ALL.

must_hit.point: Clustered index physically reorders table data (only one per table); non-clustered is a separate B-tree of pointers (many allowed).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts one clustered physical order vs many non-clustered pointer structures.

probes: LEFT JOIN/IS NULL vs NOT EXISTS — when would you pick each?
Why is LIMIT/OFFSET risky for second-highest salary?
How do RANK, DENSE_RANK, and ROW_NUMBER differ on ties?

hints.1: Think NULL-safety, tie handling, and what the engine physically does.
hints.2: Compare join-vs-exists for absences; ranking vs OFFSET for Nth; RANK gap vs DENSE_RANK no gap vs ROW_NUMBER unique.
hints.3: NOT EXISTS is NULL-safe; OFFSET can skip the wrong row on salary ties; ROW_NUMBER → 1,2,3; RANK → 1,1,3; DENSE_RANK → 1,1,2.

phases.goal: Apply advanced window/CTE patterns to gaps-and-islands, running aggregates, deletes, and classification problems.

must_hit.point: Gaps and islands: login_date minus ROW_NUMBER days yields a constant grp for consecutive login streaks; HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3 finds 3+ day streaks.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains subtracting row number as a day interval to form island groups, then filtering streak length.

must_hit.point: ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW is a running total; 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW is a rolling 7-day moving average.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate distinguishes unbounded preceding running sum from a 6-preceding-plus-current rolling average.

must_hit.point: Delete duplicates by ROW_NUMBER PARTITION BY email ORDER BY id ASC and DELETE where rn > 1, keeping the oldest id.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate keeps rn = 1 per email and deletes higher rn rows by primary key id.

must_hit.point: A cumulative sum that resets uses a running sum of (points < 0) as grp, then SUM partitioned by user_id and grp.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes incrementing grp on negatives then partitioning the running sum by that grp.

must_hit.point: Consecutive numbers: LAG and LEAD of num equal to current num identify the middle of a 3-row streak.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate uses LAG/LEAD so num matches both prev and next, then DISTINCT.

probes: How do you find users who logged in for 3 or more consecutive days?
How do you compute a running total and a 7-day moving average?
How would you delete duplicate emails while keeping one row?

hints.1: These lean on window framing and grouping tricks, not just GROUP BY.
hints.2: Date minus row-number island key; ROWS BETWEEN frames; ROW_NUMBER then DELETE rn > 1; LAG/LEAD for consecutive values.
hints.3: grp = login_date - ROW_NUMBER * 1 day, HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3; UNBOUNDED PRECEDING for running sum and 6 PRECEDING for 7-day avg; DELETE ids with rn > 1; WHERE num = prev AND num = next.

tradeoffs.topic: LEFT JOIN + IS NULL vs NOT EXISTS
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Both find customers with no orders; LEFT JOIN + IS NULL is often the fastest plan, while NOT EXISTS is cleaner and strictly NULL-safe, unlike NOT IN.

tradeoffs.topic: DENSE_RANK vs MAX subquery for second-highest salary
tradeoffs.strong_answer: DENSE_RANK handles ties and extends to Nth highest; the MAX-where-less-than-max pattern is simple but rigid to second highest only. Avoid LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 because ties for highest skip the wrong row.

tradeoffs.topic: ROW_NUMBER vs RANK/DENSE_RANK for top N per group
tradeoffs.strong_answer: Use ROW_NUMBER when you need exactly N rows per group even with tied totals; RANK/DENSE_RANK can return more or fewer rows under ties.
UNION deduplicates combined results and is slower; UNION ALL keeps all duplicates and is faster.
Clustered physically reorders table data on disk (only one per table); non-clustered is a separate B-tree pointer structure (many per table).
A non-correlated subquery runs once; a correlated subquery references the outer query and runs row-by-row, often much slower.
ACID guarantees strong consistency (SQL); BASE guarantees eventual consistency and high availability (NoSQL).
Normalization organizes tables to reduce redundancy and anomalies (e.g. 1NF → 2NF → 3NF); denormalization intentionally adds redundancy back to improve read performance by avoiding expensive joins.

gotchas.trap: Using NOT IN to find rows with no match
gotchas.correction: NOT IN is plagued by NULL comparison bugs; prefer NOT EXISTS (NULL-safe) or LEFT JOIN + IS NULL.

gotchas.trap: Using LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 for second-highest salary
gotchas.correction: Ties for the highest salary make OFFSET skip the wrong row; use DENSE_RANK or MAX with salary < max salary.

gotchas.trap: Using RANK or DENSE_RANK when you need exactly N rows per group
gotchas.correction: Ties inflate or distort counts; use ROW_NUMBER() so exactly N rows return per partition.

gotchas.trap: Confusing RANK and DENSE_RANK on ties
gotchas.correction: RANK leaves a gap (1, 1, 3); DENSE_RANK does not (1, 1, 2); ROW_NUMBER always assigns distinct 1, 2, 3.

gotchas.trap: Division by zero in year-over-year growth
gotchas.correction: Wrap the LAG prior amount with NULLIF(..., 0) so a prior-year amount of exactly 0 does not crash.

gotchas.trap: Swapping odd/even seat rows when the last id is odd
gotchas.correction: If id is odd and equals MAX(id), leave it unchanged because the last student has no pair to swap with.
Applying functions to indexed columns in WHERE (e.g. WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2026) forces a full table scan.

gotchas.trap: Thinking a View always stores data
gotchas.correction: A View is a stored query acting as a virtual table and stores no data itself unless it is a Materialized View.
